title: How do you know a service is up and running (health endpoints, heartbeats, service registry, Kubernetes probes, monitoring, gateway checks)?
shortTitle: How do you know a service is up and running
keyPoints: Liveness answers whether the process is healthy or stuck and should be restarted
Readiness answers whether the instance can actually accept traffic right now
Heartbeats to a service registry prove ongoing life but have a small staleness gap
Kubernetes probes operationalize health endpoints to restart or remove pods from rotation
Gateway and load-balancer health checks independently drop unhealthy instances from routing
Monitoring with Prometheus, Grafana, and synthetic checks close the loop with alerts and dashboards
Up is not a single flag but a hierarchy: alive, ready, dependencies healthy, end-to-end success

s1_definition.oneliner: A service is known to be up through layered signals: liveness and readiness endpoints, registry heartbeats, Kubernetes probes, gateway health checks, and monitoring alerts, not from the fact that it once started.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Liveness endpoint** – answers whether the process is healthy or stuck and should be killed and restarted.
- **Readiness endpoint** – answers whether the instance can accept traffic right now, checking real dependencies like the database.
- **Heartbeat** – the service periodically renews its lease with a service registry; missed heartbeats trigger eviction.
- **Kubernetes probes** – poll health endpoints to restart stuck containers (liveness) or remove not-ready pods from traffic (readiness).
- **Gateway health check** – the load balancer independently polls each backend and drops unhealthy instances from rotation.
- **Monitoring and alerting** – Prometheus scrapes metrics, Grafana visualizes dashboards, and PagerDuty pages the on-call engineer.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants to be sure the loans department is actually open and working. It is not enough that someone unlocked the door this morning. A supervisor walks by every few minutes and asks the clerk "are you alive and at your desk?" (liveness check) and "are you ready to take a customer right now, or still setting up?" (readiness check). The clerk also phones reception regularly to say "still here" (heartbeat to the registry). If the clerk stops answering, the supervisor sends them home and brings a replacement (Kubernetes restart), reception stops directing customers to that desk (registry eviction), and the branch manager's dashboard flashes a warning (monitoring).

sections.s6_takeaway:
Knowing a service is up means relying on objective, continuous signals rather than assuming it is fine because it started once. The most important distinction is between liveness and readiness. Liveness answers whether the process is healthy or stuck and should be restarted, while readiness answers whether the instance can actually serve traffic right now. A well-built readiness check verifies real dependencies, so readiness means genuinely able to serve, not merely running.

On top of the service's own endpoints there are heartbeats to a service registry, where the instance periodically renews its lease and the registry evicts it if several heartbeats are missed. Kubernetes probes operationalize the endpoints: the liveness probe restarts a stuck container, the readiness probe removes a not-ready pod from traffic without killing it, and a startup probe gives a slow JVM time to boot. Gateway and load-balancer health checks independently poll each backend and drop anything unhealthy from rotation, providing defense in depth.

At National Bank of India, the payment service process was alive but its database pool had silently broken, so every request failed while every basic health light stayed green. With separate liveness and readiness, liveness correctly kept the process running while readiness pulled the instance out of rotation until the dependency recovered. Monitoring with Prometheus, Grafana dashboards, and PagerDuty alerts closed the loop.

Remember one sentence: up is not a single flag but a hierarchy: alive, ready, dependencies healthy, end-to-end requests succeed, and someone is alerted the instant any layer degrades.
